prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical discovery of the Z2 topological insulator and the quantum spin Hall state, and for its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize on B006 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Having read the full first round and the chair's questions, I find the scientific case unchanged and the competing objections answerable. The distinction from 2016 can be stated in one sentence: the 2016 prize recognised topological phase transitions and topological invariants in one-dimensional chains and in the quantum Hall effect, where time-reversal symmetry is broken; the Kane-Mele Z2 invariant shows that a time-reversal-invariant band insulator with spin-orbit coupling can be topologically non-trivial and carries protected helical edge states, and Molenkamp's HgTe experiment showed those channels as quantised conductance in a real device. That is a different class of matter with a different measurement signature, and about two decades of independent transport, ARPES and STM work have settled the interpretation. Maturity is not in question. The citation as drafted is deliberately tied to the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation, so it does not imply that the three-dimensional materials discovery is being recognised. I did not change my configuration this round; my only earlier change, from Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, stands, and nothing in round 1 argues for reversing it.
statement.case_against: Three names cannot cover the field. The citation is honest about what it recognises, but it leaves Hasan and the first three-dimensional ARPES observations outside, and it leaves out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, whose HgTe proposal Molenkamp's experiment tested (Zhang is deceased). A reader can fairly say that the experimental half of the credit is thin relative to the whole experimental field. The 2016 overlap is a judgment, not a proof, and Johansson and Lindroth are right that the committee must state the distinction rather than assume it. B047, the main alternative, has a cleaner two-person attribution and I cannot rule out that its distinctness from the 2005 and 2012 prizes is stronger than non-specialists can see.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether a configuration that drops a theory co-author in order to credit two experimentalists is consistent with how the committee has handled equal co-originators, and argues that Hasan's 3D claim is partly carried by Kane and Mele through the Fu-Kane-Mele theory.
responses.response: I accept the argument and it is the reason I moved. My opening trio treated Hasan as the representative of the 3D discovery, but the Kane-Mele papers are a joint foundational work, and I cannot give a principled reason for crediting one author and not the other. Your point that the 3D prediction and observation form a theory-plus-experiment story in which the theory is already carried by Kane and Mele is the strongest answer to the Hasan question. I do not claim to answer it fully: Hasan's observation was a real experimental milestone, and I would rather the committee record that cost openly than hide it. If a member argues that Hasan, not Mele, is the more consequential name, I would want to hear it, but nobody has yet made that case persuasively.

responses.point: Kroll argues that magic-wavelength lattice trapping is a new principle, not tuning, that the lattice clock solves the problem of using many neutral atoms with no first-order light shift, and that the prize should not wait for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: This answers the chair's question as well as it can be answered by a colleague outside metrology, and I find it convincing as a statement of distinctness: combs supply the counting gearwork and ion control supplies a single-system standard, whereas the lattice clock gains from interrogating many atoms with motional and light-shift errors suppressed. I agree entirely that the committee should not wait for the metrology bodies. Where I still prefer B006 is the breadth of the discovery, not the quality of B047: topological insulators changed what a whole community of condensed-matter and materials physicists measure and compute, and clocks are concentrated in metrology and tests of constants. That is a ranking argument, and I accept that it is not decisive. I also take your point that the ion-clock community has an adjacent claim; I cannot adjudicate it, which is one reason B047 is my first alternative, not a rejected one.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B006 as her first alternative because the attribution among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and the HgTe proposers is not defensible by default, and says strength of opening support is not the same as an attribution the committee can defend.
responses.response: I agree that support counts are not the argument, and several round-1 moves followed colleagues' reasoning, so the count of six should not be read as six independent judgments. On attribution, the point I would put to you is that the three-name cut is now stable and principled: the co-authors of the founding Z2 and quantum spin Hall papers plus the experimentalist who first observed the effect, with the citation restricted to the 2D discovery. The omissions are real, but they are omissions of later or adjacent strands, and I think the committee can defend them in writing. On the 2016 worry, I hope the one-sentence distinction in my case_for resolves it for you; if it does not, tell me what else you would want in the citation.

responses.point: Johansson says the increment over the 2016 prize must be argued rather than assumed, and accepts that a second superconducting-circuit award right after 2025 would be hard to justify, and says B047 could be a later year or a second part if the union of names stays within the ceiling.
responses.response: I accept the burden and have tried to meet it in my case_for: time-reversal symmetry and spin-orbit coupling define a different class of insulator from the Chern-type and 1D cases honoured in 2016. On the two-part idea, I checked it: B006 with B047 gives Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori and Ye, which is five people, and shrinking B006 to two names would reintroduce exactly the Kane-Mele or Molenkamp omission we have just argued is hard to defend. I therefore do not propose a two-part prize this year. I note and appreciate your disclosure on B038, and I agree with you on timing.

responses.point: Olsson says IceCube's two-name credit compresses a collaboration of hundreds plus AMANDA and Baikal predecessors, and that the source identifications are still statistically modest, so B048 should wait.
responses.response: I agree with the substance, and it is why I do not propose B048 even though my background makes it the entry I understand best. As an instrument builder I know that crediting Halzen and Karle alone for a detector built by hundreds is the hardest attribution problem on the list, and the source identifications still need more statistics. The diffuse flux is a real discovery, and I would expect it to return in a later year, but I would not carry it to a vote now. I also note your shared institution with Johansson; I do not think it affects your reasoning on B006.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the citation, narrowed to the quantum spin Hall effect and its first observation, is a sufficiently honest statement given the omission of Hasan and of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang.
Whether the one-sentence distinction from the 2016 prize satisfies Johansson and Lindroth, or whether some members will still hold that the room for a second topological prize is reduced.

Whether optical lattice clocks (B047) are a stronger and more clearly distinct invention than non-specialists can judge; I cannot test the magic-wavelength argument independently and rely on Kroll and Lindroth.
I rely on general knowledge of the priority sequence for the Z2 theory, HgTe and 3D observations and have not independently verified it.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B006, B047 or B017; I have no documented connection to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori or Ye. My astroparticle background is closest to B048 (IceCube), which I ranked second in my opening ballot and am not proposing; my documented collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGOLite/PoGO+, XL-Calibur) do not include IceCube, but I continue to flag the proximity so colleagues can weigh my views on B048 accordingly. Unchanged from round 1.
